newsitem.title: KUWAIT: INTERVIEW-Kuwait NIC seeks projects abroad.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Kuwait NIC seeks projects abroad.

text.p: The Kuwait-based National Industries Co, one of the Arab world's largest listed firms, is seeking new projects and aquisitions abroad to meet an ambitious target of raising industrial assets to $1 billion by 2005.
But Kuwaiti red-tape and slow decision-making could force the Kuwait Stock Exchange-listed firm, capitalised at over $1.2 billion, to seek investment opportunities abroad.

"We set a target of spending 25 million dinars ($82.5 million) on industrial ventures in the first year (of the 10- year plan). In fact we doubled that when we bought BI," NIC Chief General Manager Robert Kottritsch told Reuters on Tuesday.

The company, which last year paid $154 million for the aquisition of the Birmingham-based BI Group PLC, on Tuesday reported a 27 percent rise in 1996 net profit to $84 million. Industrial assets are currently valued at some $300 million.

Kottritsch said that Kuwait, which has been steadily recovering from the 1990-91 Iraqi occupation, is "two years too late" in setting up government bodies to attract industrial projects and investment in the tiny Gulf Arab state.
They are "still very, very young organisations" which could take several years to implement new policies.
"In our view we have no option but to seek investment opportunities in industry" abroad.

"We are not in control of the Kuwait situation," he said of the firm which is often described as the largest and most successful to be privatised under the government's programme which was launched in September 1994.
Bahrain and Qatar are likely locations for NIC's plans to expand either through new aluminium and steel projects or seek stakes in existing projects which aim to grow.
NIC is already active in Qatar, raising its stake in February in a $400 million Qatar Steel Company hot briquetted iron project to 16.33 percent from 4.5 percent.

Iron ore "pelletisation is definitely one of the things demanding our attention over the next six months" but an earlier plan to build an aluminium smelter either in Kuwait, Qatar or elsewhere in the oil-rich region is not on the firm's list of priorities until the end of the year, added Kottritsch.
Along with America's Raytheon Co, NIC was seeking a stake in a $1 billion aluminium project in Kuwait but it is now on hold awaiting the state's decision on the price for power.
"Seventy percent of the cost of aluminium is power" and without an attractive price investors are not willing to go ahead with project, added Kottritsch.

Also Kuwait's long-awaited decision on a proposed $1.5 billion aromatics project is affecting NIC's desire to make intermediary products in Kuwait from the plant's output along with that from the $2 billion Equate Petrochemicals Co project which is due to come onstream this August.

Kottritsch says NIC, seen as the region's second largest industrial group after the much larger global giant Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC), sees downstream petrochemicals projects in Kuwait as "very interesting" but all the required ingredients are not yet in place.
So in the meantime NIC will seek major industrial investment opportunities abroad to increase the share of return from industrial projects to 75 percent of total income.

"If you look at a year ago, over three-quaters of our income is coming from our financial investments. We do not intend to reduce the size but what we are doing is leveraging...so that eventually...three-quarters of income comes from operations."
NIC -- which makes building material in Kuwait, plastic fittings and detergents -- has over $300 million invested abroad with international fund managers.
The state currently has a 1.5 percent stake in NIC while Kuwait's pension fund -- Public Institution for Social Security -- is the largest single shareholder with seven percent.
The rest is held by Kuwaiti investors.
